claim: Nematodes populate a wide variety of distinct ecological niches but only have a few sensory neurons available to encode multiple modalities.
source: Animals with small nervous systems have a limited number of sensory neurons that must encode information from a changing environment. This problem is particularly exacerbated in nematodes that populate a wide variety of distinct ecological niches but only have a few sensory neurons available to encode multiple modalities.
evidence: This is a general statement about nematode biology that draws from established scientific understanding of nematode nervous systems.

claim: P. pacificus likely lacked bilateral asymmetry according to Hong et al., 2019.
source: Previously we showed that P. pacificus likely lacked bilateral asymmetry (Hong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous publication.

claim: The salt responses of P. pacificus are encoded in a left/right asymmetric manner in the bilateral ASE neuron pair.
source: Here, we show that by visualizing neuronal activity patterns, contrary to previous expectations based on its genome sequence, the salt responses of P. pacificus are encoded in a left/right asymmetric manner in the bilateral ASE neuron pair.
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal activity visualization data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Several free-living and parasitic nematode species have nearly identical numbers of 12–13 pairs of head sensory neurons, known as the amphid neurons.
source: Several free-living and parasitic nematode species examined by serial section electron microscopy have nearly identical numbers of 12–13 pairs of head sensory neurons, known as the amphid neurons (Hong et al., 2019; Ward et al., 1975; Li et al., 2001; Bumbarger et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies using electron microscopy.

claim: The olfactory preferences of P. pacificus are distinct from those of C. elegans and the human parasite Strongyloides stercoralis.
source: As expected from their association with insects in the wild, the olfactory preferences of P. pacificus are distinct from those of C. elegans and the human parasite Strongyloides stercoralis (Hong and Sommer, 2006; Chaisson and Hallem, 2012; Hallem et al., 2011), but little is known about P. pacificus responses to water-soluble compounds.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous comparative studies.

claim: In C. elegans, the main salt receptor neuron class comprises of a bilateral pair of left and right ASE neurons (ASEL and ASER), which serve to induce an attractive locomotory response toward an increase in salt concentration.
source: In C. elegans, the main salt receptor neuron class comprises of a bilateral pair of left and right ASE neurons (ASEL and ASER), which serve to induce an attractive locomotory response toward an increase in salt concentration (Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The gene che-1 encodes a transcription factor that is exclusively expressed in the ASE neurons and is required for their proper differentiation in C. elegans.
source: The gene che-1 (chemosensory defective) encodes a transcription factor that is exclusively expressed in the ASE neurons and is required for their proper differentiation, such that a che-1 mutant results in defective salt attraction (Dusenbery et al., 1975; Uchida et al., 2003; Chang et al., 2003; Etchberger et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on C. elegans che-1.

claim: The left and right ASE neurons in C. elegans asymmetrically express receptor-type guanylyl cyclases (rGCs, encoded by gcy genes).
source: The left and right ASE neurons asymmetrically express receptor-type guanylyl cyclases (rGCs, encoded by gcy genes) (Yu et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The left and the right ASE neurons in C. elegans differentially respond to distinct salt ions.
source: This finding led to the realization that the ASE neurons are lateralized, such that the left and the right ASE neurons differentially respond to distinct salt ions (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 2001; Chang et al., 2004; Suzuki et al., 2008; Ortiz et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The miRNA lsy-6 is at the top of the gene regulatory network that programs the distinct sensory potentials of the left and right ASE neurons in C. elegans.
source: This observation led in turn to the identification of a complex gene regulatory network that genetically programs the distinct sensory potentials of the left and right ASE neurons (Hobert, 2014), which includes a miRNA, lsy-6, at the top of this gene regulatory network (Hobert, 2014; Johnston and Hobert, 2003; Cochella and Hobert, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The lsy-6 miRNA evolved selectively in the Caenorhabditis genus and is absent in P. pacificus.
source: However, the lsy-6 miRNA evolved selectively in the Caenorhabditis genus (Ahmed et al., 2013) and is absent in P. pacificus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and genomic observation.

claim: P. pacificus does not show an expansion of the ASEL-type and ASER-type rGCs, as C. elegans does.
source: Moreover, P. pacificus does not show an expansion of the ASEL-type and ASER-type rGCs, as C. elegans does (Hong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous genomic study.

claim: Ammonium salts (NH4Br, NH4Cl, and NH4I) are the strongest attractants to wildtype P. pacificus J4 to adult hermaphrodites.
source: In this survey, we found ammonium salts to be the strongest attractants to wildtype P. pacificus J4 to adult hermaphrodites (NH4Br, NH4Cl, and NH4I), with NH4I significantly more attractive to P. pacificus compared to C. elegans (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 1.

claim: NH4I is significantly more attractive to P. pacificus compared to C. elegans.
source: In this survey, we found ammonium salts to be the strongest attractants to wildtype P. pacificus J4 to adult hermaphrodites (NH4Br, NH4Cl, and NH4I), with NH4I significantly more attractive to P. pacificus compared to C. elegans (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative behavioral data shown in Figure 1.

claim: P. pacificus is less attracted to NaCl and LiCl compared to the ammonium salts.
source: Notably, in contrast to C. elegans (Ward, 1973), we find that P. pacificus is less attracted to NaCl and LiCl compared to the ammonium salts (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1 and comparison to a previous study.

claim: P. pacificus is repulsed by acetate salts (NaAc and NH4Ac), which induce attractive responses in C. elegans.
source: Also, P. pacificus is repulsed by acetate salts (NaAc and NH4Ac), which induce attractive responses in C. elegans (Frøkjaer-Jensen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and citation to a previous study on C. elegans.

claim: P. pacificus and C. elegans display differences in their salt preferences.
source: We conclude that P. pacificus and C. elegans display differences in their salt preferences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The 5′ region of the Pristionchus che-1 ortholog directs reporter expression to the Ppa ASE and Ppa AFD neuron classes.
source: Re-examination of our provisional cell identifications using a newly generated che-1p::GFP strain with stronger neurite expression revealed highly elaborated finger-like dendritic endings in the more anterior amphid neuron that could unambiguously be assigned to the AFD neurons (Figure 2A–C), prompting us to reassign expression of che-1 to ASE and AFD.
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The che-1 reporter transgene indicates the full expression of the endogenous che-1 locus.
source: We confirmed that the che-1 reporter transgene indicates the full expression of the endogenous che-1 locus by tagging the endogenous che-1 locus with an ALFA-tag (Igreja et al., 2022). The che-1::ALFA animals showed staining in 2 pairs of head neurons whose position is consistent with being the ASE and AFD neurons (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ALFA-tag immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D, E.

claim: Ppa-che-1 autoregulates its own expression especially in the ASE neurons.
source: By crossing the che-1 reporter transgene into a che-1 mutant background (see below), we also found that che-1 autoregulates its own expression especially in the ASE neurons (Figure 2F, GFP expression in 97% in WT (n = 36) vs 4% in che-1(−) (n = 48)), as it does in C. elegans (Etchberger et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data in mutant background shown in Figure 2F and citation to C. elegans study.

claim: In C. elegans, the OTX homeodomain transcription factor TTX-1 is a terminal selector expressed in the AFD neurons required for designating the AFD fate.
source: In C. elegans, the OTX homeodomain transcription factor TTX-1 is a terminal selector expressed in the AFD neurons required for designating the AFD fate (Satterlee et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study on C. elegans.

claim: Ppa-ttx-1p::RFP is strongly expressed in a pair of neurons with the hallmark finger-like dendritic ending of the AFD neurons.
source: We found ttx-1p::RFP to be strongly expressed in a pair of neurons with the hallmark finger-like dendritic ending of the AFD neurons (Figure 2G, H), as well as expression in other head and tail neurons (possibly RIP and RIB) and cells likely to be the pharyngeal marginal cells based on likely conservation with Cel-ttx-1 expression (Reilly et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 2G, H.

claim: Endogenous TTX-1 protein expression is co-expressed with che-1p::GFP in the same anterior pair of amphid neurons.
source: To confirm that endogenous TTX-1 protein expression is co-expressed with che-1p::GFP, we examined C-terminally tagged ttx-1:ALFA animals and found co-localization in the same anterior pair of amphid neurons, but no co-expression in the posterior pair of amphid neurons (Figure 2I, J, n = 15).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2I, J.

claim: Both Ppa-che-1 alleles exhibited defects in attraction toward NH4Cl and LiCl compared to wildtype.
source: Both Ppa-che-1 alleles exhibited defects in attraction toward NH4Cl and LiCl compared to wildtype (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ppa-che-1 mutants showed no detectable difference in responses to NH4I, NaCl, and NaAc.
source: However, unlike in C. elegans, Ppa-che-1 mutants showed no detectable difference in responses to NH4I, NaCl, and NaAc.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data comparing mutant and wildtype responses.

claim: Histamine-treated che-1p::HisCl1 animals showed complete loss of attraction to NH4Br, NH4Cl, and NH4I but did not significantly alter their repulsive response to NaAc.
source: Histamine-treated che-1p::HisCl1 animals showed complete loss of attraction to NH4Br, NH4Cl, and NH4I but did not significantly alter their repulsive response to NaAc (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal silencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NaAc is sensed by neurons other than ASE or AFD.
source: These findings corroborate that NaAc is sensed by neurons other than ASE (or AFD, in which the che-1 promoter also drives HisCl1).
evidence: This is inferred from the neuronal silencing data showing no effect on NaAc response.

claim: When 250 mM NH4Cl is administered, an 'ON' response is observed as calcium transiently increases in the left ASE neuron (ASEL).
source: Specifically, we looked for changes in calcium levels immediately after the addition and removal of specific salts. When 250 mM NH4Cl is administered, an 'ON' response is observed as calcium transiently increases in the left ASE neuron (ASEL).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: An 'OFF' response was observed as calcium sharply dips in the right ASE neuron (ASER) before quickly returning to baseline when NH4Cl was removed.
source: In contrast, an 'OFF' response was observed as calcium sharply dips in the right ASE neuron (ASER) before quickly returning to baseline when the salt was removed, which suggests hyperpolarization of this neuron (Figure 4A, B; Suzuki et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: When presented with 25 mM NH4Cl, the 'OFF' response completely disappeared in ASER while the 'ON' response became more pronounced in ASEL.
source: However, when presented with a tenfold lower concentration of 25 mM NH4Cl, the 'OFF' response completely disappeared in ASER while the 'ON' response became more pronounced in ASEL.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data comparing different concentrations.

claim: ASER responses to 250 and 25 mM NaCl were very similar to the 'OFF' response observed for NH4Cl.
source: The ASER responses to 250 and 25 mM NaCl (Figure 4D) were very similar to the 'OFF' response (including hyperpolarization) observed for NH4Cl, but the ASEL responses differ between the two salts: instead of the 'ON' response expected of ASEL, we observed a relatively weak 'OFF' response without the characteristic hyperpolarization but accompanied by an attenuated 'bump', a profile that we classify as an 'OFF-2' response (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: ASEL showed a strong 'ON' response to NH4I, and ASER showed an 'ON–OFF' biphasic response to 250 mM NH4I.
source: Finally, we examined the response to NH4I and found that it also elicited laterally asymmetric responses, but yet again distinct from the responses to both NH4Cl and NaCl, with ASEL showing a strong 'ON' response, and ASER showing an 'ON–OFF' biphasic response to 250 mM NH4I (Figure 4E, F; Kato et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4E, F.

claim: P. pacificus ASE neurons clearly show left/right asymmetric responses to salt attractants.
source: Altogether, P. pacificus ASE neurons clearly show left/right asymmetric responses to salt attractants and these asymmetric responses show similarities and differences to the C. elegans ASE taste neurons (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the calcium imaging data presented in Figure 4.

claim: AFD neurons responded with a distinctly 'ON–OFF' biphasic response to all three salt types at both concentrations.
source: Surprisingly, we detected a distinctly 'ON–OFF' biphasic response to all three salt types at both concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: AFD responses were more robust than ASER toward 25 mM NH4Cl, NaCl, and NH4I.
source: Specifically, although we observed weaker or comparable responses in AFD neurons when compared to either ASE neuron's response toward 250 mM NH4Cl, NaCl, and NH4I (Figure 5A, B, E, F, I, J), the AFD responses were more robust than ASER toward 25 mM NH4Cl, NaCl, and NH4I (Figure 5D, H, L).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: AFD neurons responded strongly to 25 mM NaCl when neither one of the ASE neurons showed a positive response.
source: Specifically, AFD neurons responded strongly to 25 mM NaCl when neither one of the ASE neurons showed a positive response (Figure 5G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5G, H.

claim: Ppa-gcy-22.3 is expressed exclusively in ASER.
source: We fused the promoter of one of these paralogs, Ppa-gcy-22.3, to gfp and found that transgenic animals express GFP exclusively in ASER (Figure 6A), identical to the C. elegans gcy-22 ortholog (Ortiz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Expression of gcy-22.3 was eliminated in che-1(ot5012) mutants.
source: To assess whether Ppa-gcy-22.3 is a potential effector of Ppa-che-1 function, we crossed the gcy-22.3 reporter into che-1(ot5012) mutants. We found expression of gcy-22.3 was eliminated (Figure 6C), leading us to conclude that gcy-22.3 is a potential effector of che-1 function, identical to its homolog in C. elegans.
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data in mutant background shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The 'OFF' response to 250 mM NH4Cl was notably abolished in the ASER neuron in the loss-of-function gcy-22.3 mutant, while the 'ON' response in the ASEL remained intact.
source: The 'OFF' response to 250 mM NH4Cl was notably abolished in the ASER neuron in the loss-of-function gcy-22.3 mutant, while the 'ON' response in the ASEL remained intact (Figure 7B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data in mutant background shown in Figure 7B, C.

claim: The responses to 250 mM NaCl were not significantly reduced in either the ASEL or ASER neuron in the gcy-22.3 mutant.
source: However, the responses to 250 mM NaCl were not significantly reduced in either the ASEL or ASER neuron in the gcy-22.3 mutant (Figure 7D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data in mutant background shown in Figure 7D, E.

claim: The gcy-22.3 mutation reduced the 'ON' portion of the AFD biphasic response following presentation of 250 mM NH4Cl and NaCl.
source: Furthermore, the gcy-22.3 mutation also reduced the 'ON' portion of the AFD biphasic response following presentation of 250 mM NH4Cl and NaCl (Figure 7F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data in mutant background shown in Figure 7F, G.

claim: No significant differences were found between wildtype and gcy-22.3 mutants in responses toward individual ions, except that attraction to NH4Cl was slightly enhanced in both alleles.
source: We also examined the behavioral responses toward individual salt ions in gcy-22.3 mutants, including a second loss-of-function allele csu182. Overall, we found no significant differences between wildtype and mutants in responses toward individual ions, and only the attraction to NH4Cl was slightly enhanced in both alleles (Figure 8), which was unexpected given the lack of calcium response observed in gcy-22.3(csu181) toward NH4Cl.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8.

claim: While proper ASE function is critical for salt attraction, defects in individual gcy genes do not lead to a major impact on the worms' ability to track toward attractive salts.
source: Our findings show that while proper ASE function is critical for salt attraction, defects in individual gcy genes do not lead to a major impact on the worms' ability to track toward attractive salts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and calcium imaging data on gcy-22.3 mutants.

claim: Functional lateralization in P. pacificus may be mediated by a different genetic pathway compared to C. elegans.
source: Our unexpected discovery that neuronal asymmetry is present in the ASE homologs between two distantly related nematode species, despite the lack of a lsy-6 homolog, suggests that functional lateralization in P. pacificus may be mediated by a different genetic pathway compared to C. elegans.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of lateralization despite absence of lsy-6.

claim: While C. elegans is attracted to acetate salts, P. pacificus avoids these acetates.
source: We have shown that while C. elegans is attracted to acetate salts, P. pacificus avoids these acetates.
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral data presented earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Ammonium acetate (NH4Ac) is sensed both as a water-soluble compound as well as a volatile odorant and is mediated by different signaling pathways in C. elegans.
source: Previous studies have shown that ammonium acetate (NH4Ac) is sensed both as a water-soluble compound as well as a volatile odorant and is mediated by different signaling pathways (Frøkjaer-Jensen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study on C. elegans.

claim: The P. pacificus ASEL neuron responds to a decrease in NaCl concentration (likely sodium), whereas the C. elegans ASEL neuron responds to an increase in sodium concentration.
source: The P. pacificus ASEL neuron responds to a decrease in NaCl concentration (likely sodium), as evidenced by the 'OFF-2' response profile, whereas the C. elegans ASEL neuron responds to an increase in sodium concentration.
evidence: This is a comparison based on calcium imaging data and previous C. elegans studies.

claim: In both P. pacificus and C. elegans, the ASER neuron responds to a decrease in chloride concentration.
source: However, in both nematodes, the ASER neuron responds to a decrease in chloride concentration.
evidence: This is a comparison based on calcium imaging data and previous C. elegans studies.

claim: The P. pacificus ASER neuron exhibits a unique ON–OFF response to ammonium iodide, whereas in C. elegans, no ON–OFF type of response is seen in the ASE neurons.
source: Additionally, the P. pacificus ASER neuron exhibits a unique ON–OFF response to ammonium iodide, whereas in C. elegans, no ON–OFF type of response is seen in the ASE neurons – the C. elegans ASER neuron responds only to a decrease in iodide concentration.
evidence: This is a comparison based on calcium imaging data and previous C. elegans studies.

claim: Attraction to ammonium ions (NH4+) is likely mediated in part by the ASER neuron in P. pacificus.
source: Based on our calcium imaging and chemotaxis results on the gcy-22.3 mutants, attraction to ammonium ions (NH4+) is likely mediated in part by the ASER neuron in P. pacificus.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium imaging and behavioral data on gcy-22.3 mutants.

claim: Pristionchus species are entomophilic and most frequently found to be associated with beetles in a necromenic manner.
source: Pristionchus species are entomophilic and most frequently found to be associated with beetles in a necromenic manner and thus insect cadavers could be sources of ammonium in the soil (Koneru et al., 2016; Herrmann et al., 2007; Herrmann et al., 2006; Fielding et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous ecological studies.

claim: In P. pacificus, nutritional state has a measurable role in the mouth-form polyphenism decision between predatory and non-predatory morphs.
source: In P. pacificus, nutritional state has a measurable role in the mouth-form polyphenism decision between predatory and non-predatory morphs (Piskobulu et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The sensitivity range of the P. pacificus ASER responses is significantly less compared to the ASEL responses, as well as to C. elegans ASER responses.
source: The sensitivity range of the P. pacificus ASER responses is significantly less compared to the ASEL responses, as well as to C. elegans ASER responses.
evidence: This is a comparison based on calcium imaging data.

claim: The C. elegans ASER has a 40-fold sensitivity range in the 'OFF' response to the removal of various concentrations of NaCl (1–40 mM).
source: Whereas the C. elegans ASER has a 40-fold sensitivity range in the 'OFF' response to the removal of various concentrations of NaCl (1–40 mM) (Suzuki et al., 2008; Rabinowitch et al., 2014; Shindou et al., 2019; Watteyne et al., 2020), the P. pacificus ASER showed the 'OFF' response only to 250 mM NH4Cl but not to a tenfold reduction in concentration of NH4Cl (25 mM).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous C. elegans studies.

claim: The narrower sensitivity range in P. pacificus chemosensation was also observed for attraction to volatile odors, which span only 10-fold, versus up to 10,000-fold in attractive odors for C. elegans.
source: The narrower sensitivity range in P. pacificus chemosensation was also observed for attraction to volatile odors (Hong and Sommer, 2006), which span only 10-fold, versus up to 10,000-fold in attractive odors for C. elegans (Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In C. elegans, hyperosmotic stimulus such as 1 M glycerol, or high concentrations or long duration of CuSO4 exposure both result in biphasic responses by the ASH neurons that sense noxious chemicals.
source: In C. elegans, hyperosmotic stimulus such as 1 M glycerol, or high concentrations or long duration of CuSO4 exposure both result in biphasic responses by the ASH neurons that sense noxious chemicals (Wang et al., 2015; Chronis et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous C. elegans studies.

claim: C. elegans olfactory neurons that mediate avoidance behavior such as the AWB neurons can exhibit a biphasic response to the presence and removal of a high concentration isoamyl alcohol that normally elicits avoidance behavior.
source: Olfactory neurons that mediate avoidance behavior such as the AWB neurons can also exhibit a biphasic response to the presence and removal of a high concentration isoamyl alcohol that normally elicits avoidance behavior (Yoshida et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous C. elegans study.

claim: C. elegans chemosensory neurons have been classically characterized as specialized neurons for dedicated modalities.
source: Broadly speaking, C. elegans chemosensory neurons have been classically characterized as specialized neurons for dedicated modalities such as water-soluble chemicals (ASE), volatile odorants (AWA, AWB, and AWC), noxious chemicals (ASH), pheromones (ADL, ADF, and ASK), and light (ASJ) and temperature (AFD) (Bargmann, 2006; Bargmann et al., 1993; Mori and Ohshima, 1995; Sengupta et al., 1996; Macosko et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous C. elegans studies.

claim: Advances in multi-neuron calcium recordings have shown that a given odor within a certain concentration range is detected by different ensembles of the 12 amphid neuron classes, including the AFD neurons.
source: Advances in multi-neuron calcium recordings have since shown that a given odor within a certain concentration range is detected by different ensembles of the 12 amphid neuron classes, including the AFD neurons (Leinwand and Chalasani, 2013; Lin et al., 2023; Yemini et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies using calcium imaging.

claim: The loss of the receptor gcy-22.3 reduced the AFD 'ON' response to NH4Cl and NaCl, indicating ASER contributes to the AFD response.
source: Moreover, the loss of the receptor gcy-22.3 reduced the AFD 'ON' response to NH4Cl and NaCl, indicating ASER contributes to the AFD response.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium imaging data in gcy-22.3 mutants.

claim: The integration of thermosensation and chemosensation is important for memory-regulated behavior.
source: The integration of thermosensation and chemosensation is important for memory-regulated behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: In C. elegans, maximum chemotaxis indices toward NH4Cl occurs when there is concordance between cultivation temperature and assay temperature.
source: In C. elegans, maximum chemotaxis indices toward NH4Cl occurs when there is concordance between cultivation temperature and assay temperature (Kuhara et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous C. elegans study.

claim: The C. elegans AFD neurons are important for gustatory aversive learning in NaCl avoidance.
source: The C. elegans AFD neurons are also important for gustatory aversive learning in NaCl avoidance (Watteyne et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous C. elegans study.

claim: The key regulator of Cel ASE identity, che-1, is also expressed in Ppa ASE and may play a similar role as a terminal selector in this neuron type.
source: We found that the key regulator of Cel ASE identity, che-1, is also expressed in Ppa ASE and may play a similar role as a terminal selector in this neuron type, based on its effect on ASE-mediated behavior and regulation of the Ppa-gcy-22.3 gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression data and functional studies.

claim: A developmental loss of ASE differentiation may result in compensatory changes in the chemosensory system during early development, as was observed in the C. elegans mating pheromone response by males.
source: It is possible that a developmental loss of ASE differentiation may result in compensatory changes in the chemosensory system during early development, as was observed in the C. elegans mating pheromone response by males (White et al., 2007).
evidence: This is speculation based on a previous C. elegans study.

claim: Cel-gcy-22 stands out for being located on a separate chromosome (Chr. V) compared to the other ASER-type gcy genes (gcy-1, gcy-4, gcy-5 on Chr. II).
source: It is also worthwhile to note that Cel-gcy-22 stands out for being located on a separate chromosome (Chr. V) compared to the other ASER-type gcy genes (gcy-1, gcy-4, gcy-5 on Chr. II) as well as the Cel-gcy-22 mutant having defects in chemoattraction toward a wide range of salt ions (Ortiz et al., 2009; Ortiz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on C. elegans gcy genes.

claim: The five P. pacificus gcy-22-like paralogs are located on three separate chromosomes (Chr. I, IV, and X), likely emerging from independent and repeated gene duplication events after the separation of Caenorhabditis and Pristionchus lineages.
source: Given that the five P. pacificus gcy-22-like paralogs are located on three separate chromosomes (Chr. I, IV, and X), it is likely that they emerged from independent and repeated gene duplication events after the separation of Caenorhabditis and Pristionchus lineages.
evidence: This is inferred from genomic data on gene locations.

claim: Unlike in C. elegans, the Ppa-che-1 gene is also expressed in the AFD neurons.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that unlike in C. elegans, the Ppa-che-1 gene is also expressed in the AFD neurons.
evidence: This is based on expression data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The miRNA lsy-6 is apparently lacking in P. pacificus, representing the most striking difference in the gene regulatory architecture of ASE neuron specification.
source: Perhaps the most striking difference in the gene regulatory architecture of ASE neuron specification is the apparent lack of the key regulator of ASE asymmetry in P. pacificus, the miRNA lsy-6.
evidence: This is based on genomic observations.

claim: In C. elegans, the expression of lsy-6 exclusively in ASEL is prepatterned via an early embryonic Notch signal.
source: In C. elegans, the expression of lsy-6 exclusively in ASEL is prepatterned via an early embryonic Notch signal (Cochella and Hobert, 2012) and serves to downregulate the homeodomain transcription factor cog-1 in the ASEL neuron (Johnston et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous C. elegans studies.

claim: cog-1 and several asymmetrically expressed downstream effectors of cog-1, such as the die-1, lim-6, and fozi-1 transcription factors are conserved in P. pacificus.
source: cog-1 and several asymmetrically expressed downstream effectors of cog-1, such as the die-1, lim-6, and fozi-1 transcription factors are conserved in P. pacificus, but whether the function of these factors in controlling P. pacificus ASE laterality is conserved remains to be determined.
evidence: This is based on genomic conservation data.

claim: Another prominent gene regulatory pathway that is controlled by miRNAs in C. elegans, the heterochronic pathway (let-7s and lin-4), appears to have diverged in P. pacificus as well, despite the conservation of the overall physiological readouts of this pathway.
source: In this context it is intriguing to note that another prominent gene regulatory pathway that is controlled by miRNAs in C. elegans, the heterochronic pathway (let-7s and lin-4), appears to have diverged in P. pacificus as well, despite the conservation of the overall physiological readouts of this pathway (temporal patterning of cell lineage divisions) (Sharma et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: miRNA-meditated regulatory process is particularly labile.
source: It is tempting to speculate that miRNA-meditated regulatory process is particularly labile.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed divergence in miRNA pathways.
